groups.title: When the data changes
groups.blurb: The shop depends on feeds sent by other teams and companies. A feed can change format, arrive late or arrive broken.

scenarios.title: A late feed is reported and the rest still loads
scenarios.promise: When a feed does not arrive, the team is told, and every other report still loads on time.

related.why: When a feed is not just late but broken, an operator can leave it out of the nightly load.

scenarios.title: One broken feed must not stop every report
scenarios.promise: When one feed arrives broken, an operator skips it for tonight and every other report is still on time.

related.why: The skip list is another setting an operator can change in a minute, without a new release.

scenarios.title: Messy test data is fine in development, never in production
scenarios.promise: The same check only warns while we try things out, and stops the load where real customers depend on it.

scenarios.title: Switching to a new scan format on an agreed day
scenarios.promise: The carrier changes its scan format on one day, and we switch on that day, so no parcel scan goes missing.

related.why: The switch day is a setting an operator can change without a new release, like the skip list in that scenario.

groups.title: When the code changes
groups.blurb: Every change to the reports is rehearsed, checked and kept tidy before it can reach anyone.

scenarios.title: Every change is rehearsed in a sandbox before it is accepted
scenarios.promise: A mistake in a proposed change is caught by an automatic rehearsal, long before any report is wrong.

scenarios.title: Sloppy or risky code is refused before it is saved
scenarios.promise: A robot tidies every change and refuses known bad habits, so reviewers can focus on the content.

scenarios.title: Every developer works on their own copies
scenarios.promise: Three developers can build the same table at the same time without overwriting each other.

groups.title: When we release
groups.blurb: New versions reach the shop in a fixed order, can be pulled back in seconds and cannot be changed in secret.

scenarios.title: A bad release is undone in seconds
scenarios.promise: Going back to yesterday's version is changing one number, not repairing anything.

related.why: This is where the numbered versions are explained. Here a second version is made for you while the demo gets ready.

scenarios.title: A fix made by hand in production is detected
scenarios.promise: Before every release the stack compares the real database with the code and stops on hand-made changes.

scenarios.title: Every environment runs one exact, numbered version
scenarios.promise: The question 'which version is running in production?' always has one exact answer.

scenarios.title: Take one team's change out of a release
scenarios.promise: When one team is not ready, only that team's change waits and the other team ships.

related.why: Each finished change gets a version number. The unfinished one is taken out by its number.

scenarios.title: The robot that builds development cannot touch production
scenarios.promise: Each environment has its own robot with keys to its own rooms only, so a mix-up cannot damage production.

groups.title: Every day
groups.blurb: The nightly load runs on its own. When it fails, people get one clear mail and a fast way back.

scenarios.title: Every run and every check is written down
scenarios.promise: The question "what ran last night, how long did it take, what failed" always has an answer, in plain tables.

related.why: The mail reports tonight's failure; the record keeps the history of every night.

scenarios.title: A failed night produces one clear mail
scenarios.promise: When the nightly load fails, the team gets one short mail that says what failed, not a wall of text.

related.why: After reading the mail and fixing the cause, only the failed part is run again.

scenarios.title: Rebuilding a big table while people keep reading it
scenarios.promise: A big table is rebuilt next to the old one and swapped in at once, so readers never see an empty table.

scenarios.title: After a fix, only the failed part runs again
scenarios.promise: When a night fails and the cause is fixed, the retry redoes only what failed and what waits for it.

related.why: The mail tells the team what failed, so they know what to fix before they retry.

glossary.database: The big, organised store where all the shop's data lives, in tables.
glossary.environment: One complete copy of the system with its own data. We have three: development (trying things), validation (checking) and production (the real one).
glossary.feed: Data that another team or company sends us again and again, for example the carrier's parcel scans or customer reviews.
glossary.hand-made change: A change someone typed straight into the live database instead of putting it through the normal, recorded route.
glossary.log: The diary a program writes while it works: one line for every step, in the order it happened.
glossary.model: One table of the shop's reports, built from raw data by a small piece of code.
glossary.nightly load: The job that runs every night and rebuilds all the shop's reports from the latest data.
glossary.operator: The person who keeps the nightly load running, not the person who writes the reports.
glossary.release: A bundle of finished changes that goes live together on an agreed day.
glossary.robot account: A login used by a program instead of a person. It has its own keys that only open certain doors.
glossary.sandbox: A private scratch copy where a change can be tried without touching what others use.
glossary.setting: A value an operator can change in a minute to alter tonight's nightly load, without building anything new.
glossary.table: One sheet of the database: rows and columns, like a page of a spreadsheet.
glossary.test: An automatic check on the data, for example that every order has a number.
glossary.version: One exact, numbered state of all our code, for example v1.0.2. Like the edition number of a book.
